paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Dewey, Oklahoma, was an attack, reported in early 1919, in which a mob destroyed the homes of Black men and women at Dewey and drove them from the town. It is known from the Black press of Oklahoma, where Oklahoma City Black leaders cited it in an address to the Governor and the attorney W. H. Twine brought a bill to reimburse the victims.

The coverage gives no date for the attack and reports no cause or accusation against the residents. When the earliest report appeared on February 14, 1919, the attack was described as having happened "only recently."

According to the address to the Governor, a mob at Dewey destroyed the homes of "more than twenty of our most law abiding citizens," confiscated their property, and drove them from the city. The signers noted that some of these residents had sons in France fighting for the nation. No deaths or injuries were reported, and no member of the mob was named.

The address, signed by Roscoe Dunjee, editor of the Black Dispatch, Dr. A. Baxter Whitty of the Oklahoma City NAACP, and others, urged the Governor to act against lynching and to speak publicly for the safety of Black citizens. In early March the Black Dispatch reported that Twine had come to Oklahoma City to place before the legislature a bill to reimburse the black men and women whose homes had been destroyed. Twine gave a copy of the bill to each Republican member of the house and senate. No report of the bill's fate, of arrests, or of any prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Black Dispatch and the Bookertee Searchlight printed the address on the same day, February 14, 1919, where the Dewey attack appeared in a passage on lynching that called such lawlessness "inhuman and intolerable."

On March 7 the Black Dispatch ran a front-page item headed "Twine Asks State Aid For Dewey Mob Victims." The paper cast the bill as a test of the Republican legislators, saying Black Oklahomans would watch to see whether any would be "strong and courageous enough to present this righteous petition." The attack does not appear in the coverage beyond these two Oklahoma papers.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Dewey, Oklahoma
bases: A mob destroyed the homes of more than twenty Black residents, confiscated their property and drove them from the city (A1, A2, A3); driving them out is the core act, with property destruction alongside it.

All reports come from one circle of Oklahoma City Black leaders and the Black Dispatch: the address (A1) printed again the same day (A2), and the Dispatch's item on Twine's bill (A3); none is a firsthand or local Dewey account.

accounts.label: Address of Oklahoma City Black leaders to the Governor
accounts.gist: A mob at Dewey had recently destroyed the homes of more than twenty law-abiding citizens, some with sons in France, confiscated their property and driven them from the city, bringing shame on the state.

accounts.label: Black Dispatch news item
accounts.gist: Attorney Twine brought a bill to reimburse the black men and women whose homes a mob at Dewey destroyed and who were driven from the city.

framing.detail: The address set Dewey within an appeal against lynching, calling such lawlessness 'inhuman and intolerable' and stressing the victims' loyalty and sons in France.
The Black Dispatch headlined 'Twine Asks State Aid For Dewey Mob Victims' and called the bill a 'righteous petition' testing Republican courage.
